answer.rationale:
memory_c2 is the load-bearing memory here: it is the only record that would justify moving primary supply to the low-cost vendor, and the low-cost quote alone satisfies the 18% mandate, so a single decision cycle could be spent on a full switch on the strength of that one consolidated line. That is exactly why it needs the archive pull. As consolidated, c2 attests to unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy — it is conspicuously silent on on-time delivery, fill rate, quality escapes, and the volume band the switch covered. Cost and billing hygiene are not delivery reliability. With the line at 94% of committed volume and zero buffer, a migration that is merely 'quick to onboard' is not the same as one that never missed a ship date, and the consolidated form cannot tell me which it was. It may also describe a smaller or non-critical component rather than primary supply at current volumes.

Until that is resolved, I intend to negotiate terms with the incumbent, using the low-cost quote as the benchmark. This is supported by memory_c4 (benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and terms) and memory_c6 (term length unlocked volume pricing without narrowing service scope), and it is the only direction that pursues the mandate without putting untested delivery performance in front of a line with no slack. memory_c1 supports the low-risk side: renewal preserved integration stability with no migration work. I am treating negotiation as the guarded move, not the final answer — the aim is a term structure that captures a meaningful share of the 18% while keeping the low-cost vendor alive as a qualified second source for a scoped trial at the next review, which is where memory_c3's second-sourcing benefit would properly apply.

Risk I am explicitly flagging downstream: if I switch now and c2 turns out to rest on a low-volume or non-critical engagement, the cost saving gets booked immediately while the delivery failure surfaces weeks later, and the next agent inherits 'switching to low-cost vendors works' as a twice-confirmed lesson with the failure attributed to execution. That compounding is worse than missing part of the mandate this cycle. If the archive shows c2 covered primary supply at comparable volume with clean delivery performance, I will escalate the low-cost vendor to a scoped primary trial next cycle rather than treat negotiation as the end state. If negotiation lands well short of 18%, I will report the shortfall as a shortfall rather than close it by accepting unverified delivery risk.
